summary: Describes the EPP mapping for provisioning and managing host names, such as name servers, in a shared central repository. It defines how EPP commands and responses work for host objects, in XML. It was replaced by RFC 4932.

eli5.summary: Computers that answer for domain names need their own entries. This part of the registry language says how to add, change and look up those entries.

questions: how are name servers registered in epp
subtitle: How to register and manage DNS nameserver entries in the EPP registry system.

tldr.problem: Domain registries need a standardized way to provision, retrieve, and manage the DNS nameserver host entries that domains delegate to.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines the EPP mapping for host objects, which allows registrars to create, update, query, and delete host records in a central registry using standardized XML commands.
tldr.outcome: Registries can manage nameserver records consistently with other EPP operations, keeping hosts in sync with the domains they serve. RFC 4932 updated this specification.

today: RFC 4932 updated this specification in May 2007 with clarifications and enhancements to the EPP host mapping.

sections.title: Introduction and Host Objects
sections.content:
The Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP, defined in RFC 3730) is a standardized protocol for provisioning objects in domain registries. This document describes the EPP mapping for host objects—the records that represent DNS nameservers and other hosts used for delegating domains.

A host object has a subordinate relationship to domain objects in the registry. For example, the host ns1.example.com belongs to the domain example.com. EPP actions like transfers must preserve this relationship. However, a host can also be an external host, meaning it does not belong to the namespace of the repository where it is being used (for example, ns1.external.net used as a nameserver for a domain in the .example repository).
sections.eli5: When you register a domain, it needs to point to computers that answer questions about it. Those computers are called nameservers. The registry keeps a list of them. This describes how to add and change them.

sections.title: Host Object Attributes
sections.content:
Every EPP host object stores several key attributes:

  • Host name: A fully qualified domain name conforming to standard DNS naming rules. Names may be internationalized using the IDNA standard.
  • IP addresses: Zero or more IPv4 or IPv6 addresses for the host. When provisioning a nameserver, IP addresses are included only as needed to generate DNS glue records—additional address records that help clients bootstrap the DNS lookup.
  • Status values: Each host has status flags set by the sponsoring client or the server, such as ok (normal), linked (associated with another object), clientUpdateProhibited (client cannot modify it), or pendingCreate (creation is in progress pending human review).
  • Dates and times: Creation date, last update date, and last transfer date, all in UTC using the format specified in RFC 3339.
  • Client identifiers: The sponsoring client and the client that created the object.
  • Repository Object Identifier (ROID): A unique server-assigned identifier for the host.
sections.eli5: The registry keeps track of the host name, what IP addresses it has, whether it is locked from changes, and when it was created or changed.

sections.title: EPP Command Mapping
sections.content:
EPP defines two kinds of commands: query commands and transform commands. For hosts, EPP provides:

Query commands: The <check> command tests if a host name can be provisioned (is available) in a repository. The <info> command retrieves all details about an existing host object. Transfer queries do not apply to hosts because hosts cannot be transferred directly; they are transferred implicitly when their superordinate domain is transferred.

Transform commands: The <create> command creates a new host object with a name and optional IP addresses. The <delete> command removes a host, but only if it is not associated with any domain. The <update> command modifies a host: it can add or remove IP addresses or status values, or change the host name entirely (subject to server policies and client restrictions).

All commands use XML and follow the standard EPP envelope format. Servers MUST return response codes indicating success (1000) or special conditions like pending human review (1001).
sections.eli5: You can ask the registry if a nameserver name is available, get its details, create one, delete one, or change its addresses.

sections.title: Management and Pending Actions
sections.content:
Host objects can have a pendingCreate, pendingDelete, pendingTransfer, or pendingUpdate status, indicating that a transform command has been received but the server has not yet completed the action. This allows registry operators to perform human review or third-party verification before actually modifying the object. Once the offline review is complete, the server sends a service message to the client indicating success or failure.

When a host name changes, it can affect other objects (like domains) that refer to it. Most such references are automatically preserved, except when updating an external host that is referenced by domains sponsored by different clients—in that case, the server MUST reject the update, and the client must create a new host with a new name and update the referring objects.

All date-time values in EPP responses MUST be in UTC with the extended format (e.g., 1999-04-03T22:00:00.0Z). The protocol uses Unicode and UTF-8 encoding for internationalized domain names and multilingual status messages.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the registry needs human approval before actually adding or changing a nameserver. The registry tells you when the action is done. If you rename a host that is used by other domains, you have to update those domains too.
